summary: Provides a framework of scenarios and requirements for pseudowire (PW) redundancy. A set of redundant pseudowires is configured between provider edge nodes, and the nodes need to agree on which one carries traffic. It is informational.

eli5.summary: If one road to school closes, you want a spare road ready. This memo lists the situations and rules for having backup roads for network connections and switching safely.

subtitle: Scenarios and requirements for keeping an emulated network service alive with backup pseudowires.

tldr.problem: If an attachment circuit or a provider edge node fails, the emulated service carried over a pseudowire can lose connectivity, and protection in the packet switched network cannot cover every failure.
tldr.mechanism: A set of redundant pseudowires is configured, and a new Preferential Forwarding Status of active or standby lets the edge nodes agree on the one pseudowire that carries traffic.
tldr.outcome: The RFC gives six reference scenarios and generic requirements for protection switching and operations. It is a framework, and the signaling mechanisms are specified elsewhere.

today: RFC 6718 is an Informational RFC from August 2012 and, according to the unit metadata, is not obsoleted or updated. It is a framework of scenarios and requirements, and the signaling that carries the status is specified elsewhere.

sections.title: Why Pseudowire Redundancy
sections.content:
The objective of pseudowire (PW) redundancy is to maintain connectivity across the packet switched network (PSN) if a component in the path of the emulated service fails, or when a backup component is activated. It uses redundant attachment circuits (ACs), provider edge (PE) nodes and PWs to remove single points of failure, while ensuring that only one path between a pair of customer edge (CE) nodes is active at any time. Mechanisms that need more than one active path, such as 1+1 protection switching, are out of scope.

The PSN layer can protect a PW segment, for example with an RSVP-TE LSP with fast reroute, and this may restore connectivity quickly enough to avoid triggering PW redundancy. But PSN protection cannot cover a PE node failure or a failure of the remote AC. A CE is therefore typically dual-homed to different PE nodes. Changes on the dual-homed side must not be propagated to the ACs on the other side, and PSN failures must not be propagated to the CEs.
sections.eli5: The network already has some ways to go around broken links, but not for every kind of break. Spare connections fill the gaps, and only one is used at a time.

sections.title: Key Terms
sections.content:
• Active PW: an up PW used for user-plane, control-plane and OAM traffic. A standby PW is up but not used for user traffic, though it may forward OAM and specific control-plane traffic.
  • Primary PW: the PW a PW endpoint prefers when several qualify, set by local configuration. All other PWs in the set are secondary by default.
  • Revertive switching returns traffic to the primary PW once it is up and a wait-to-restore timer expires. Non-revertive switching keeps the last PW selected.
  • 1:1, N:1 and 1+1 protection: a standby subset protects one subset of the path (1:1), N standby subsets protect one (N:1), or traffic is permanently duplicated on both (1+1).

The RFC also defines terms from VPLS, such as MTU-s, PE-rs and n-PE, and notes that its term PE also covers T-PEs.
sections.eli5: An active road is the one cars use now, a standby road is the spare. A primary road is the favorite, and revertive means going back to the favorite when it reopens.

sections.title: PE Architecture and Forwarding Status
sections.content:
In the PE architecture of Figure 1, one AC connects to a forwarder, and the forwarder has several single PW instances. It selects which redundant PW to use. The figure is based on Figure 4b of RFC 3985.

The framework adds a new PW status, the Preferential Forwarding Status, which is active or standby. It is separate from the operational states defined in RFC 5601. It reflects the forwarding state of the ACs, so PW redundancy can make sure only one path is available from one CE to the other. The mechanisms for communicating the status are outside the scope of the document.
sections.eli5: Each PW has a flag saying "use me" or "wait". Everyone must read the flags the same way so only one road is open.

sections.title: The Six Reference Scenarios
sections.content:
The scenarios are example topologies that can be combined.

  • One dual-homed CE (3.2.1): CE1 is dual-homed to PE1 and PE3 with PW1 active and PW2 standby. If the AC to PE1 fails, the AC on PE3 becomes active, PW2 becomes active and PW1 standby, and PE2 switches to PW2. The AC status must be signaled to PE2.
  • Two dual-homed CEs (3.2.2): both CEs are dual-homed and four PWs (PW1 to PW4) are up, but only one MUST be selected to forward traffic. Each dual-homing algorithm picks its AC independently, so the active status of each AC must be signaled so the PEs choose a common PW.
  • Redundant MS-PWs (3.2.3): single-homed CEs with three multi-segment PWs switched at different S-PEs, protecting against S-PE failure (N:1 protection). The T-PEs advertise active based on a PW priority, which MUST be used if revertive mode is used, and both T-PEs should transmit over the segment switched by the same S-PE.
  • H-VPLS PE-rs (3.2.4): an MTU-s is dual-homed to PE1-rs and PE2-rs, chooses one spoke PW as active and communicates PW group status. PW grouping is recommended for scaling, and MAC Address Withdraw messages can flush MAC state.
  • VPLS ring (3.2.5): PW groups connect PEs in two VPLS domains in a ring, and exchanging a standby status lets a group be blocked at both ends, not just where RSTP blocks it.
  • VPLS n-PE (3.2.6): only one n-PE per access network is the primary. With a full mesh the primary replicates multicast, broadcast and unknown unicast frames over every core PW, wasting 67% of core bandwidth with three n-PEs and 75% with four. Exchanging active or standby PW status avoids this.
sections.eli5: The memo draws six pictures of networks with spare roads. In each one, the rule is the same: the two ends must agree on a single road, and a break on one side should not bother the other side.

sections.title: Generic Requirements
sections.content:
Protection switching: 1:1 protection MUST be supported, N:1 SHOULD be, and 1+1 MAY be used. Non-revertive behavior MUST be supported and revertive behavior is OPTIONAL. Switchover can be started by a manual or forced switch at a PE or by a signal failure; both MUST be supported, and signal failure triggers have lower priority than forced or manual triggers. A PE MAY forward packets received from a standby PW to avoid losing in-flight packets, but for VPLS all application packets from standby PWs MUST be dropped except OAM and control-plane packets.

Operations: PEs SHOULD automatically discover and try to resolve inconsistent primary/secondary or revertive/non-revertive configuration. PEs that do not MUST generate an alarm on an inconsistency. They MUST support configuring revertive or non-revertive mode if both exist, SHOULD support local invocation of protection switching and of a lockout, and the MIBs MUST support inter-PSN monitoring of the redundancy configuration.
sections.eli5: The rules say a spare must always be possible, switching can be done by a person or by a fault, and if two ends disagree on settings, someone has to be told.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The method requires an extension to the PW setup and maintenance protocol of RFC 4447, which is carried over LDP (RFC 5036). It therefore inherits the security mechanisms of the LDP version implemented in the PEs.
sections.eli5: The spare-road messages travel the same way as the normal ones, so they are protected the same way.
